instruction:
Turn the following result into an HTML visualization:
On the webarena benchmark, we evaluate the success rate (%) of different systems. 
- Baseline methods: GPT-4o (14.9), AutoEval (20.2), BrowserGym (23.5), and BrowserGym axtree (15.0)
- Our method: AWM (35.5)
- Human baseline: Step (33.0)

Visualize results in HTML on three methods on 3 splits of the Mind2Web dataset:
- cross-task split: MindAct (36.2), AWM-offline (45.1), AWM-online (43.6)
- cross-website split: MindAct (30.1), AWM-offline (33.7), AWM-online (33.9)
- cross-domain split: MindAct (26.4), AWM-offline (32.6), AWM-online (35.5)
I want to show:
1. both AWM methods (offline and online) outperforms the baseline MindAct
2. as we transfer from cross-task to website to domain settings, AWM-online gradually outperforms AWM-offline

Visualize in HTML the accuracy (%) of different models on the MMLU benchmark across four subject categories:
- STEM: GPT-4 (82.3), Claude-3 (80.1), Gemini-Pro (78.4), LLaMA-3 (71.2)
- Humanities: GPT-4 (88.5), Claude-3 (87.2), Gemini-Pro (84.3), LLaMA-3 (79.6)
- Social Sciences: GPT-4 (85.1), Claude-3 (83.7), Gemini-Pro (82.0), LLaMA-3 (76.4)
- Other: GPT-4 (83.6), Claude-3 (82.0), Gemini-Pro (80.5), LLaMA-3 (74.9)

Show that GPT-4 and Claude-3 consistently lead across all categories, while LLaMA-3 has the largest gap in STEM.

Plot the training loss curves over 100k steps for three model sizes, in HTML:
- 1B parameters: steps 0 (4.2), 10k (3.1), 25k (2.4), 50k (1.9), 75k (1.6), 100k (1.4)
- 7B parameters: steps 0 (4.2), 10k (2.8), 25k (2.0), 50k (1.5), 75k (1.2), 100k (1.0)
- 70B parameters: steps 0 (4.2), 10k (2.5), 25k (1.6), 50k (1.1), 75k (0.85), 100k (0.72)

Highlight that larger models converge to lower loss values and converge faster in early training.

Create an HTML visualization comparing human evaluation scores (1–5 scale) for text summarization systems across three dimensions:
- Fluency: Extractive (3.8), Abstractive (4.3), LLM-based (4.7)
- Coherence: Extractive (3.5), Abstractive (4.0), LLM-based (4.6)
- Faithfulness: Extractive (4.5), Abstractive (3.6), LLM-based (4.2)

Draw attention to the fact that extractive methods excel at faithfulness while LLM-based methods dominate fluency and coherence.

Here is the ImageNet top-1 accuracy (%) of major vision models since 2012. Plot the trend in HTML to show the dramatic jump from traditional CNNs to modern transformers. Only label 4–6 representative milestones.

2012: AlexNet 63.3
2014: VGG-16 74.4
2015: ResNet-50 76.1
2016: DenseNet 77.4
2017: SENet 82.7
2018: NASNet 83.0
2019: EfficientNet-B7 84.4
2020: ViT-L 85.2
2021: CoAtNet 86.0
2022: CoCa 91.0
2023: EVA-02 90.0
2024: InternViT 91.6

Plot in HTML the retrieval performance (Recall@10, %) of dense retrieval systems on three QA datasets:
- NaturalQuestions: BM25 (59.1), DPR (79.4), Contriever (84.2), BGE (88.5)
- TriviaQA: BM25 (66.8), DPR (79.8), Contriever (83.9), BGE (87.4)
- WebQ: BM25 (55.2), DPR (73.6), Contriever (79.3), BGE (84.1)

Emphasize that BM25 consistently lags behind neural methods, and BGE achieves the best results across all datasets.

Visualize in HTML the success rate (%) of robotic manipulation policies under three levels of environment noise:
- Low noise: BC (72.3), GAIL (75.1), IRL (78.4), Ours (88.2)
- Medium noise: BC (58.4), GAIL (61.7), IRL (65.3), Ours (80.6)
- High noise: BC (41.2), GAIL (44.5), IRL (49.8), Ours (71.3)

Show that our method maintains high performance even as noise increases, while baselines degrade sharply.

Create an HTML bar chart showing the inference speed (tokens/second) and memory usage (GB) of four LLMs at the same batch size. Display both metrics side-by-side per model.
- GPT-3 (175B): speed 42, memory 320
- LLaMA-2 (70B): speed 91, memory 128
- Mistral (7B): speed 310, memory 14
- Phi-2 (2.7B): speed 520, memory 6

Plot in HTML the ROUGE-L score (%) of summarization models trained on increasing amounts of data:
- 1k examples: BART (28.3), PEGASUS (30.1), T5 (29.4)
- 10k examples: BART (33.7), PEGASUS (36.2), T5 (35.8)
- 50k examples: BART (38.1), PEGASUS (40.5), T5 (40.2)
- 100k examples: BART (40.3), PEGASUS (42.7), T5 (42.5)

Show that PEGASUS consistently leads, and all models benefit substantially from more data but with diminishing returns.

Visualize in HTML the toxicity reduction (% of toxic outputs) for a language model under different safety interventions:
- No intervention: 18.4%
- Keyword filter: 12.1%
- RLHF: 6.3%
- Constitutional AI: 3.8%
- RLHF + Constitutional AI: 1.9%

Show a clear monotonic decrease, with combined methods achieving the lowest toxicity.

Show the win rate (%) of our dialogue system vs. baselines in a pairwise human preference study across four criteria:
- Engagingness: vs. Blenderbot (61%), vs. DialoGPT (67%), vs. ChatGPT (48%)
- Informativeness: vs. Blenderbot (70%), vs. DialoGPT (72%), vs. ChatGPT (52%)
- Empathy: vs. Blenderbot (74%), vs. DialoGPT (69%), vs. ChatGPT (44%)
- Overall: vs. Blenderbot (68%), vs. DialoGPT (71%), vs. ChatGPT (49%)

Note that our system underperforms ChatGPT on empathy and overall, but outperforms all other baselines.

Plot the code generation pass@1 rate (%) on HumanEval across programming languages for two systems:
- Python: CodeLlama (62.3), GPT-4 (87.1)
- JavaScript: CodeLlama (55.8), GPT-4 (79.4)
- Java: CodeLlama (51.2), GPT-4 (74.6)
- C++: CodeLlama (48.7), GPT-4 (72.1)
- Rust: CodeLlama (31.4), GPT-4 (58.3)

Emphasize that the performance gap widens for less common languages like Rust.

Here is the cumulative number of published papers on large language models per year. Plot the exponential growth trend and annotate only 3–4 key inflection points (e.g., GPT-3 release, ChatGPT release).

2017: 45
2018: 120
2019: 380
2020: 910
2021: 1820
2022: 3650
2023: 9400
2024: 21300
2025: 38700

Visualize the accuracy (%) of vision-language models on a visual question answering (VQA) benchmark broken down by question type:
- Yes/No: CLIP (82.1), BLIP-2 (87.4), LLaVA (89.2), GPT-4V (92.3)
- Number: CLIP (43.2), BLIP-2 (51.7), LLaVA (56.3), GPT-4V (63.8)
- Other: CLIP (51.4), BLIP-2 (58.2), LLaVA (63.1), GPT-4V (70.5)

Show that Number questions are the hardest for all models, and GPT-4V leads by the largest margin there.

Plot the trade-off between precision and recall for three document retrieval systems on a legal QA dataset. Use a scatter plot where each point represents a system:
- BM25: precision 71.2, recall 68.4
- Dense Retrieval: precision 74.5, recall 79.3
- Hybrid: precision 78.1, recall 80.6
- Our Method: precision 82.4, recall 83.7

Annotate the Pareto frontier and show our method is the only one in the top-right corner.

Visualize the hallucination rate (%) of LLMs on a medical QA benchmark as a function of context length (in tokens):
- GPT-4: 512 (8.2), 1024 (11.4), 2048 (15.7), 4096 (21.3)
- Claude-3: 512 (7.1), 1024 (9.8), 2048 (13.2), 4096 (17.6)
- Gemini-Pro: 512 (9.4), 1024 (13.1), 2048 (18.5), 4096 (25.2)

Show that all models hallucinate more with longer contexts, and Claude-3 is the most robust.

Plot the latency (ms) of a multi-agent system as the number of agents scales from 1 to 64:
- Synchronous: 1 (120), 2 (240), 4 (480), 8 (950), 16 (1920), 32 (3900), 64 (7850)
- Asynchronous: 1 (120), 2 (135), 4 (155), 8 (190), 16 (240), 32 (320), 64 (490)
- Our Method: 1 (120), 2 (128), 4 (142), 8 (163), 16 (195), 32 (245), 64 (360)

Highlight that synchronous latency grows nearly linearly while our method and asynchronous scale much more gracefully.

Create a radar/spider chart comparing five LLMs across six capability dimensions (scores out of 100):
- GPT-4: Reasoning (91), Coding (89), Math (88), Factuality (85), Safety (80), Instruction-following (93)
- Claude-3: Reasoning (89), Coding (85), Math (84), Factuality (88), Safety (92), Instruction-following (91)
- Gemini-Pro: Reasoning (86), Coding (84), Math (87), Factuality (82), Safety (81), Instruction-following (88)
- LLaMA-3: Reasoning (80), Coding (79), Math (76), Factuality (77), Safety (74), Instruction-following (82)
- Mistral: Reasoning (78), Coding (81), Math (74), Factuality (74), Safety (70), Instruction-following (79)

Plot the relationship between model size (in billions of parameters, x-axis, log scale) and few-shot accuracy (%) on a reasoning benchmark (y-axis):

0.3B: 24.1
1B: 31.7
3B: 40.2
7B: 51.8
13B: 59.3
30B: 68.4
70B: 76.2
175B: 83.5
540B: 88.1

Show the emergent behavior: performance grows slowly at first, then accelerates sharply beyond ~7B parameters.

Visualize reward scores across five training checkpoints for three RLHF variants:
- Standard PPO: 1k (1.2), 5k (2.1), 10k (2.8), 20k (3.1), 40k (3.2)
- PPO + KL penalty: 1k (1.1), 5k (2.3), 10k (3.1), 20k (3.5), 40k (3.6)
- Our DPO method: 1k (1.4), 5k (2.7), 10k (3.4), 20k (3.8), 40k (4.1)

Show that our DPO method achieves higher reward at every checkpoint, with the gap widening at later stages.

Show the energy consumption (kWh) and CO2 emissions (kg) for training different model sizes. Use a dual-axis bar+line chart, one axis for energy and one for emissions:
- BERT-base: energy 13, CO2 11
- GPT-2: energy 78, CO2 65
- T5-11B: energy 520, CO2 433
- GPT-3: energy 1287, CO2 1072
- LLaMA-2-70B: energy 3200, CO2 2666

Visualize question answering accuracy (%) on three domains comparing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) versus fine-tuning versus our hybrid approach:
- Open-domain: RAG (67.3), Fine-tuning (71.2), Hybrid (79.4)
- Closed-domain (Medical): RAG (54.8), Fine-tuning (63.7), Hybrid (72.1)
- Temporal (news): RAG (71.5), Fine-tuning (48.3), Hybrid (74.8)

Highlight that fine-tuning struggles severely with temporal data, while our hybrid approach is robust across all three domains.

Create a stacked bar chart showing the error breakdown (%) for a speech recognition system across four conditions. Each bar should sum to 100%.
- Clean speech: substitution (4.2), deletion (1.8), insertion (0.9), correct (93.1)
- Noisy speech: substitution (14.3), deletion (6.7), insertion (3.2), correct (75.8)
- Accented speech: substitution (18.1), deletion (5.4), insertion (2.8), correct (73.7)
- Telephone audio: substitution (21.3), deletion (9.8), insertion (5.1), correct (63.8)

Plot the user task completion rate (%) in a human-computer interaction study, comparing three UI configurations over five weeks of use (learning curve):
- Standard UI: week 1 (52.3), week 2 (61.4), week 3 (67.8), week 4 (71.2), week 5 (73.1)
- Adaptive UI: week 1 (55.1), week 2 (67.3), week 3 (75.6), week 4 (81.4), week 5 (85.2)
- Our AI-assisted UI: week 1 (63.4), week 2 (74.2), week 3 (82.1), week 4 (87.6), week 5 (91.3)

Show that our AI-assisted UI starts highest and maintains the steepest improvement slope over time.

Visualize the performance degradation (drop in accuracy, %) of models under five types of adversarial attacks:
- TextFooler: BERT (-18.3), RoBERTa (-14.2), ALBERT (-15.7), Ours (-7.4)
- PWWS: BERT (-15.1), RoBERTa (-11.8), ALBERT (-13.2), Ours (-5.9)
- DeepWordBug: BERT (-21.4), RoBERTa (-17.3), ALBERT (-19.1), Ours (-9.2)
- BERT-Attack: BERT (-24.7), RoBERTa (-19.5), ALBERT (-22.3), Ours (-10.8)
- BAE: BERT (-16.8), RoBERTa (-13.1), ALBERT (-14.9), Ours (-6.7)

Show that our model consistently suffers the smallest drop under all attack types.

Plot a heatmap of pairwise F1 (%) between six intent labels on a dialogue intent classifier (rows = true label, columns = predicted):
- Greeting→Greeting (94.2), Greeting→Farewell (2.1), Greeting→Booking (1.3), Greeting→Cancel (0.8), Greeting→FAQ (1.6)
- Booking→Greeting (1.8), Booking→Booking (91.7), Booking→Cancel (3.4), Booking→FAQ (2.1), Booking→Farewell (0.9)
- Cancel→Booking (4.2), Cancel→Cancel (89.5), Cancel→FAQ (3.1), Cancel→Greeting (1.4), Cancel→Farewell (1.8)
- FAQ→FAQ (88.3), FAQ→Booking (5.6), FAQ→Greeting (2.7), FAQ→Cancel (2.4), FAQ→Farewell (1.0)
- Farewell→Farewell (96.1), Farewell→Greeting (1.5), Farewell→Booking (0.7), Farewell→FAQ (1.2), Farewell→Cancel (0.5)
- Off-topic→FAQ (12.4), Off-topic→Greeting (8.3), Off-topic→Booking (6.1), Off-topic→Off-topic (71.2), Off-topic→Cancel (2.0)

Use a diverging color scale and annotate the diagonal. Show that Booking and Cancel are the most confused pair.

Create a Sankey diagram showing how 10,000 training examples flow through a data-cleaning pipeline into final splits:
- Raw crawl: 10,000
- After deduplication: 7,400 (2,600 removed)
- After language filter: 6,100 (1,300 removed)
- After toxicity filter: 5,200 (900 removed)
- After quality scorer (threshold 0.7): 3,850 (1,350 removed)
- Train split: 3,080 | Validation: 385 | Test: 385

Emphasize that deduplication removes the largest single share, and less than 40% of raw data reaches training.

Compare score distributions across 10 random seeds using violin plots for four RL policies on a continuous control task (success rate % per seed):
- PPO: seeds [62, 58, 71, 65, 54, 68, 61, 59, 73, 66]
- SAC: seeds [71, 74, 68, 77, 70, 72, 69, 75, 73, 71]
- TD3: seeds [68, 63, 70, 67, 64, 69, 66, 62, 71, 65]
- Ours: seeds [81, 84, 78, 86, 82, 85, 80, 83, 87, 84]

Overlay median markers. Show that Ours has the highest median and narrowest spread.

Turn this ablation into a waterfall chart starting from a random baseline and building up to the full model (accuracy %):
- Random baseline: 50.0
- + pre-training: 75.6 (+25.6)
- + data augmentation: 79.1 (+3.5)
- + attention module: 84.3 (+5.2)
- Full model (verify): 84.3

Show cumulative gains; pre-training provides the largest single step.

Visualize a hyperparameter sweep with parallel coordinates (each line = one run). Normalize scores to 0–100. Report final validation F1:
- lr=1e-5, batch=32, dropout=0.1, warmup=500 → F1 78.2
- lr=3e-5, batch=32, dropout=0.1, warmup=500 → F1 84.6
- lr=3e-5, batch=64, dropout=0.1, warmup=500 → F1 82.1
- lr=3e-5, batch=32, dropout=0.3, warmup=500 → F1 81.4
- lr=3e-5, batch=32, dropout=0.1, warmup=2000 → F1 86.9
- lr=1e-4, batch=32, dropout=0.1, warmup=500 → F1 79.8
- lr=3e-5, batch=128, dropout=0.2, warmup=1000 → F1 83.5

Highlight the best run in a distinct color. Show that warmup=2000 with moderate lr stands out.

Plot a stacked area chart of GPU memory usage (GB) over a 24-hour training run, broken down by component:
- Hour 0–6: optimizer states (42), activations (28), gradients (18), KV cache (0)
- Hour 6–12: optimizer states (44), activations (31), gradients (20), KV cache (8)
- Hour 12–18: optimizer states (46), activations (35), gradients (22), KV cache (24)
- Hour 18–24: optimizer states (48), activations (38), gradients (24), KV cache (52)

Show that KV cache memory dominates growth in the second half of training.

Create a streamgraph of topic proportions (%) in a pretraining corpus by year (topics sum to 100% each year):
- 2019: Code (18), Math (12), Science (22), News (28), Fiction (20)
- 2020: Code (22), Math (14), Science (20), News (24), Fiction (20)
- 2021: Code (26), Math (16), Science (18), News (20), Fiction (20)
- 2022: Code (31), Math (18), Science (16), News (17), Fiction (18)
- 2023: Code (38), Math (20), Science (14), News (14), Fiction (14)
- 2024: Code (45), Math (22), Science (12), News (11), Fiction (10)

Show the rising share of Code and Math at the expense of News and Fiction.

Draw a slope chart comparing model rankings on MMLU (2023 rank → 2024 rank; lower rank is better). Only include models present in both years:
- GPT-4: 2023 rank 1 → 2024 rank 3
- Claude-3: 2023 rank 4 → 2024 rank 2
- Gemini-Pro: 2023 rank 6 → 2024 rank 4
- LLaMA-2-70B: 2023 rank 5 → 2024 rank 8
- Mistral-7B: 2023 rank 12 → 2024 rank 6
- GPT-3.5: 2023 rank 8 → 2024 rank 14

Highlight upward slopes (worse rank). Show Claude-3 and Mistral-7B improved the most.

Create dumbbell charts (paired dots connected by a line) for accuracy (%) before vs. after domain-adaptive fine-tuning on five biomedical NER entity types:
- Disease: base 72.4 → adapted 89.1
- Chemical: base 68.9 → adapted 86.3
- Gene: base 74.2 → adapted 90.5
- Species: base 81.0 → adapted 92.8
- Cell line: base 63.5 → adapted 81.7

Show the largest gain on Cell line, the smallest on Species.

Plot a funnel chart for a web-navigation agent on 1,000 e-commerce tasks:
- Tasks attempted: 1000
- Valid plan generated: 842
- First action executed: 731
- Reached correct page: 524
- Completed purchase step: 318
- Order confirmed (success): 187

Label conversion % between stages. Show the steepest drop between reaching the correct page and completing purchase.

Use ridge plots (joyplot) to overlay validation loss curves across 8 seeds for three architectures (loss at epochs 1, 5, 10, 20, 40):
- LSTM: all seeds start ~4.8–5.0, epoch 40 range 2.1–2.8
- Transformer-S: all seeds start ~4.5–4.7, epoch 40 range 1.4–1.9
- Transformer-L: all seeds start ~4.2–4.4, epoch 40 range 0.9–1.2

Show that Transformer-L ridges are narrowest at epoch 40 (most stable across seeds).

Plot a hexbin density chart of 2,400 (prompt length tokens, human helpfulness score 1–5) ratings for an LLM assistant:
- Densest bin center: length 120, score 4.2, count 310
- Secondary cluster: length 45, score 4.5, count 185
- Sparse long-prompt tail: length 3500+, scores mostly 2.0–3.1
- Overall correlation: r = -0.42

Add a smoothing trend line. Show that very long prompts correlate with lower helpfulness.

Create a connected scatter plot (trajectory) for three retrieval systems across scaling index size (million docs) on x and Recall@10 (%) on y:
- BM25: 1M (78.2) → 10M (71.4) → 100M (63.8)
- Dense: 1M (82.5) → 10M (80.1) → 100M (77.6)
- Ours: 1M (85.3) → 10M (84.7) → 100M (83.9)

Use arrows between points. Show BM25 degrades sharply at scale while Ours stays nearly flat.

Build a Marimekko (mosaic) chart: x-width = share of 2024 API traffic by model family, y-height = outcome mix within each family (all % within family sum to 100):
- Open-weight (38% of traffic): success 72, refusal 18, error 10
- Closed API tier-1 (34%): success 86, refusal 9, error 5
- Closed API tier-2 (20%): success 79, refusal 14, error 7
- Fine-tuned enterprise (8%): success 91, refusal 6, error 3

Show that enterprise fine-tunes are a small traffic slice but the highest success proportion.

Draw a chord diagram of cross-task transfer (F1 gain % when fine-tuned on source then evaluated on target; only show flows ≥8%):
- NER→RE: 12.4
- NER→QA: 9.1
- QA→NER: 8.7
- QA→Summarization: 14.2
- Summarization→QA: 11.8
- RE→NER: 10.3
- RE→QA: 9.6
- Summarization→NER: 8.2

Thickness encodes gain. Show QA→Summarization is the strongest transfer link.

Plot a polar area (coxcomb) chart of monthly share of total inference spend (%) for a research lab in 2024 (months sum to 100%):
- Jan 6.2, Feb 7.1, Mar 8.4, Apr 9.0, May 10.2, Jun 11.5, Jul 12.8, Aug 11.9, Sep 9.6, Oct 8.3, Nov 7.4, Dec 7.6

Show spend peaking mid-year (Jun–Jul) during large-scale pretraining.

Create bullet charts for three production SLAs (target / actual / poor threshold):
- P50 latency (ms): poor >300, target 180, actual 142
- Availability (%): poor <99.0, target 99.9, actual 99.94
- Cost per 1M tokens ($): poor >6.0, target 3.5, actual 2.8

Show all three metrics exceed targets with comfortable margin.

Plot overlapping histograms with KDE curves for perplexity on a held-out set for two language models:
- Base model: bins centered at [2.8, 3.2, 3.6, 4.0, 4.4, 4.8] with counts [85, 210, 340, 290, 150, 45]
- Instruction-tuned: bins centered at [2.0, 2.4, 2.8, 3.2, 3.6, 4.0] with counts [120, 380, 410, 220, 90, 30]

Use transparency. Show the instruction-tuned distribution shifted left (lower perplexity).

Plot a Gantt-style timeline (horizontal bars) for a 70B model training schedule:
- Data prep: day 0–14
- Pretrain phase 1 (4k ctx): day 14–80
- Pretrain phase 2 (32k ctx): day 80–162
- Mid-training cooldown: day 162–175
- SFT: day 175–195
- RLHF: day 195–210
- Eval & red-team: day 210–220

Color phases differently. Show pretraining dominates wall-clock.

Use a horizon chart (compact layered areas) to compare four metrics over 20 training epochs (0–19) for one run:
- Train loss: starts 3.8, ends 1.1 (monotonic decrease)
- Val loss: starts 3.9, min 1.3 at epoch 14, ends 1.5 (slight uptick)
- Val accuracy (%): starts 42, ends 89, peak 90 at epoch 14
- Gradient norm: starts 2.4, spikes 5.1 at epoch 3, stabilizes ~0.8 after epoch 10

Normalize each metric to 0–1 for display. Show early overfitting signal: val loss bottoms at epoch 14 then rises while train loss keeps falling.

Plot a lollipop chart ranking ten embedding models by MTEB average score (%) — only show top and bottom five for clarity:
- E5-large-v2: 64.8
- BGE-large-en: 63.5
- GTE-large: 62.9
- OpenAI-ada-002: 60.1
- Instructor-XL: 59.4
- GloVe-840B: 38.2
- Universal-Sentence: 41.5
- MiniLM-L6: 48.7
- all-MiniLM-L12: 51.3
- TF-IDF baseline: 32.4

Sort descending. Show the gap between neural embedders and TF-IDF.

Create a bump chart of leaderboard rank (1=best) over four benchmark rounds for five agents on WebArena:
- Round 1: AWM 1, AutoEval 3, BrowserGym 2, GPT-4o 4, Human 5
- Round 2: AWM 1, BrowserGym 2, AutoEval 4, GPT-4o 3, Human 5
- Round 3: AWM 1, GPT-4o 2, BrowserGym 3, AutoEval 4, Human 5
- Round 4: AWM 1, GPT-4o 2, BrowserGym 4, AutoEval 3, Human 5

Minimize line crossings. Show AWM stays rank 1 while GPT-4o climbs from 4 to 2.

Draw a population-pyramid-style diverging bar chart for human vs. model annotation disagreement rates (%) across ten error categories:
- Left (human over-predicts): Hallucination 8.2, Omission 5.4, Wrong entity 4.1, Temporal 6.8, Coreference 3.2
- Right (model over-predicts): Hallucination 2.1, Omission 9.6, Wrong entity 7.3, Temporal 1.4, Coreference 5.9

Categories on the y-axis. Show Omission and Wrong entity skew toward model over-prediction.

Plot a candlestick-style chart (open/high/low/close) for daily benchmark score volatility over one week on GAIA (higher is better):
- Mon: O 41.2 H 43.8 L 40.1 C 42.6
- Tue: O 42.6 H 44.1 L 41.9 C 43.5
- Wed: O 43.5 H 45.0 L 42.8 C 44.2
- Thu: O 44.2 H 46.3 L 43.7 C 45.8
- Fri: O 45.8 H 48.1 L 45.2 C 47.4

Show four consecutive bullish days (close > open) with widening highs.

Use a sunburst chart for hierarchical compute usage on one training job:
- Total GPU-hours: 10,000
- Pretrain: 7,200 (Forward 4,100, Backward 2,400, Optimizer 700)
- Data loading: 1,400 (Tokenize 900, Disk I/O 500)
- Checkpointing: 900
- Logging & eval: 500

Inner ring = top level, outer ring = sub-components. Show forward pass dominates pretrain.
